title: Zero boil-off storage of cryogenic hydrogen in orbit
bottleneck: Liquid hydrogen boils at -253 C, just 20 degrees above absolute zero, and no insulation is perfect: heat from sunlight and radiation constantly leaks in, vaporizing propellant and pressurizing the tank. A NASA analysis found a large liquid-hydrogen tank carrying 38 tons would passively lose roughly 16 tons per year — the fuel would boil away long before a Mars mission departed. Preventing this needs active zero-boil-off cooling (cryocoolers, jet mixing, droplet injection) running reliably for months.
why_it_blocks: Every beyond-Earth-orbit architecture — lunar landers, Mars transfer stages, orbital depots — depends on stockpiling cryogenic propellant for weeks to months. Without long-duration storage, multi-launch refueling architectures cannot accumulate the propellant they need.
current_state: NASA's Robotic Refueling Mission 3 demonstrated zero-boil-off techniques, and active-cooling approaches exist as lab hardware. Depot-scale, months-long demonstration in orbit has not flown.
